slides.say: A circle has a radius of root thirty-five centimeters. Its central angles go alpha, beta, alpha, beta, five of each, like in the figure. One alpha sector and one beta sector are shaded. What's their total area?

slides: Now, here's the thing. We can't find alpha or beta on their own. And actually, we don't even need to.

slides.say: Let's look at the shaded part. It's one alpha and one beta, sitting right next to each other, right?

slides: So what do I need? The shaded part is just a piece of the circle. So I need two things. First, the area of the whole circle. And second, how much of the circle is shaded.

slides.say: The area of a circle is pi r squared. Here r is root thirty-five, and root thirty-five squared is just thirty-five, because the square cancels the root. So the whole circle is equal to thirty-five pi.

slides: Now, how much of it is shaded? For that I need alpha and beta, and they don't give me a single number. So what can I say about them?

slides.say: Let's count them. Here are the five alphas. Now here are the five betas. And together, they go all the way around the circle. So five alpha plus five beta is equal to three hundred sixty degrees.
Now look at this side. One equation, two unknowns. So I can't get alpha or beta on its own, right? But I can get their sum.
I just divide both sides by five. Or take out five as a common factor, it's the same thing. So alpha plus beta is equal to seventy-two degrees.

slides: Could they be thirty and forty-two? Sure. Could they be twelve and sixty? Also. It doesn't matter, because all I need is their sum.

slides.say: Now remember, a sector takes the same part of the circle's area as its angle takes out of three hundred sixty degrees. Together, the two shaded sectors are seventy-two out of three hundred sixty degrees. And seventy-two over three hundred sixty is one fifth.
at: seventy-two out of three hundred sixty

slides: So the shaded part is one fifth of thirty-five pi. That's seven pi.

slides.say: So number two is our answer. You see, we never found alpha or beta. We only needed their sum. So whenever you can't find each one on its own, look for their sum. I'll see you in the next question.
